ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -023, -030, -035 thru -066
BLM’s Motion to Sever and Dismiss Group 1 Appeals
and Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Jurisdiction Denied
Now pending and fully briefed are BLM’s Motion to Sever and Dismiss Group 1
Appeals (Guerry Motion) and Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Jurisdiction (JRS Motion).
These motions pertain to two groups of grazing decisions: (1) decisions issued February
28, 2020 (Group 1) and decisions issued June 15, 2020 (Group 2). For the reasons set
forth below, those motions are denied.
The Guerry Motion seeks dismissal of Docket Nos. ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -023,
and -030, which involve appeals by Western Watersheds Project (WWP) and WildLands
Defense (WLD) of February 28, 2020, grazing decisions issued to the grazing permittee,
Guerry, Inc., for the Coonskin-EJD and Pigtail Butte Allotments (Allotments). JRS
Properties III LLLP (JRS), another grazing permittee of the Allotments, was granted
intervenor party status in those cases.
The JRS Motion seeks dismissal of Docket Nos. ID-JFO-2020-043, -045, -048, -064,
and -066, which involve appeals by WWP, WLD, and JRS of June 15, 2020, grazing
decisions issued to JRS for the Allotments. JRS was granted intervenor party status in
the appeals of WWP and WLD.
JRS was granted intervenor party status in the appeals of the Group 1 decisions
affecting the Allotments (Docket Nos. ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -023, and -030) by Order
dated September 3, 2020. That Order also consolidated the appeals of the Group 1
decisions and the Group 2 decisions affecting the Coonskin-EJD Allotment (Docket Nos.
ID-JFO-2020-006, -023, -043, -046, -064) and consolidated the Group 1 decisions and the
Group 2 decisions affecting the Pigtail Allotment (Docket Nos. ID-JFO-2020-013, -030,
-045, -048, -066).
For the appeals of the Cookskin-EJD Allotment decisions, that Order reasoned as
follows regarding consolidation and JRS’s intervention in the appeals of the Guerry
decision:
Given that both decisions establish a single integrated grazing
scheme with a single deferment schedule, single set of range
improvements, and single set of Objectives, Management Guidelines,
Thresholds, and Responses for a single allotment, there is great
commonality of facts pertinent to all appeals of the decisions. The
commonality of issues is also great, as all, or nearly all, the issues raised
13

ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -023, -030, -035 thru -066
by WWP and WLD pertain to both decisions. Thus, consolidation of all
the Coonskin-EJD appeals is clearly warranted.
JRS’s intervention in the appeals relating to Guerry’s permit is also
warranted because, as a practical matter, JRS’s interests in grazing the
allotment would be impaired if a decision unfavorable to its positions
regarding the integrated grazing management scheme is entered in those
appeals. JRS’s positions include the assertion that this scheme established
in both decisions lacks a rational basis and will not work as intended, thus
harming JRS’s interests.
. . . .
In fact, because BLM has designed an integrated system of grazing
management for the allotment, DCHD would arguably be bound to issue
rulings regarding the decisions which are consistent, or it would
otherwise effectively implement a new, judge-made grazing decision
without the benefit of public input or BLM analysis and with potentially
unintentional adverse consequences to the environment or the permittees.
See WWP v. BLM, 195 IBLA 115, 123-24 (2020). Taking such action is not in
the public interest, see id. at 124, and amounts to managing the public
lands as a proxy for BLM, which DCHD does not have authority to do, S.
Utah Wilderness Alliance, 172 IBLA 183, 184-85 (2007).
These principles bolster the conclusion that the rulings to be made
regarding Guerry’s permit are inextricably linked to the rulings to be
made pertaining to JRS’s permit. Consequently, rulings regarding
Guerry’s permit may impair JRS’s interests and JRS’s intervention in the
appeals pertaining to Guerry’s permit for the Coonskin-EJD Allotment is
justified.
Sept. 3, 2020 Order at 8-9. For similar reasons, JRS was granted intervenor status in the
appeals of the Pigtail Butte Allotment decision issued to Guerry and the appeals
regarding the Pigtail Butte Allotment were consolidated.
Later, the appeals of the Group 1 decisions were consolidated and the appeals of
the Group 2 decisions were consolidated. All ten dockets pertaining to the Allotments
were consolidated with both the consolidated appeals pertaining to the Group 1
decisions and the consolidated appeals pertaining to the Group 2 decisions because
BLM’s stated rationale for the Group 1 decisions is not the same as its stated rationale
14

ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -023, -030, -035 thru -066
for the Group 2 decisions, necessitating JRS’s involvement in both groups of appeals to
protect its interests for those ten dockets. See Orders dated March 17, 2021, and April
19, 2021.
Then, the parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment regarding the
appeals pertaining to the Group 1 decisions. In addressing briefing of the summary
judgment motions, this Tribunal declined to limit the briefing to specific issues.
By Orders dated August 9, 2021, this Tribunal granted summary judgment to
BLM regarding the consolidated appeals of the Group 1 decisions. Neither WWP nor
WLD appealed the order granting summary judgment against it.
In the Guerry Motion, BLM seeks (1) severance of the four dockets pertaining to
the Group 1 decisions affecting the Allotments (Docket Nos. ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -
023, and -030) from the consolidated Group 2 appeals and (2) dismissal of those four
dockets. BLM argues that the August 9, 2021 Orders granting summary judgment to
BLM on the WWP and WLD Group 1 appeals and the subsequent failure of WWP and
WLD to appeal those orders results in BLM’s Group 1 decisions becoming final. BLM
therefore requests that the appeals be severed from the Group 2 appeals and dismissed.
In the JRS Motion, BLM argues that the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction over the six
dockets pertaining to the Group 2 decisions affecting the Allotments (Docket Nos. ID-
JFO-2020-043, -045, -048, -064, and -066) because JRS limited its summary judgment
briefing for the appeals of the Group 1 decisions to certain issues, that BLM was granted
summary judgment on those issues in the August 9, 2021 Order, and that the Interior
Board of Land Appeals now has jurisdiction over the matters by virtue of JRS’s appeal
of the August 9, 2021 Order. BLM argues that “JRS Properties did not raise other issues
that it could have in its Group 1 briefs, and it may not unilaterally do what the Hearings
Division declined to do, which is limit the issues to be litigated [in the Group 1]
proceeding, while reserving the right to maintain arguments for another day [in the
Group 2 proceeding].”
JRS persuasively argues that both motions should be denied:
. . . BLM’s Guerry Motion should be denied because JRS has party status
via its intervenor status in such four (4) dockets and JRS remains to have
such party status to further adjudicate such dockets in the above-noted
JFO Group 2 dockets (which is currently subject to a cross-motion for
summary judgment process).
15

ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -023, -030, -035 thru -066
And, BLM’s Guerry Motion and BLM’s JRS Motion should be
denied because the Hearings Division decided in the ALJ Orders dated
March 17, 2021 and April 19, 2021, to consolidate and to have concurrent
jurisdiction over such ten (10) dockets relative to the Hearings Division
adjudication of such dockets in JFO Group 1 and in JFO Group 2.1
Assuming, however, the Hearings Division (now) finds that it cannot have
concurrent jurisdiction over the six (6) docket numbers subject to BLM’s
JRS Motion, then the Hearings Division should issue an Order -- either
directing the BLM / JRS to move the Board or requesting the Board on its
own Order -- to suspend the Board’s jurisdiction over IBLA-2021-0335
pending the Hearings Division’s concurrent jurisdiction and adjudication
of JFO Group 2 dockets as to such six (6) docket numbers so the currently
pending JFO Group 2 summary judgment motion process and
adjudication process can continue and not be delayed as to, at least, the
ten (10) dockets at issue.
“RESPONSE BY JRS PROPERTIES III LLLP TO (1) BLM’s ‘Motion to Sever and Dismiss
Group 1 Appeals Pertaining to the Coonskin-EJD and Pigtail Butte Allotments’ dated
October 12, 2021, and (2) BLM’s ‘Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Jurisdiction’ dated
October 12, 2021” at 4-5.
In other words, JRS did not lose its party status in the four dockets pertaining to
the Group 1 decisions when WWP and WLD chose not to appeal the orders granting
summary judgment and the four dockets remain active with respect to JRS’s
contentions as part of the Group 2 appeals. The four dockets were consolidated with
both the Group 1 consolidated appeals and the Group 2 consolidated appeals. The
Group 2 appeals and JRS’s contentions remain pending regarding the integrated
grazing scheme approved in both the four Group 1 dockets and the six Group 2 dockets
pertaining to the Allotments. THEREFORE, THE GUERRY MOTION IS DENIED.
Regarding the JRS Motion, BLM elaborates on its argument:
Management on the ground with respect to the JRS Properties
decisions is currently stayed based on a stipulation BLM agreed to at the
onset of the appeals before the Hearings Division. However, that stay
does not extend past the issuance of a final order resolving the appeal at
the Hearings Division. After that, a party must file a new petition for stay
at the IBLA or enter into a new stipulation with BLM. The practical
consequence of having an appeal in two tribunals is that BLM is not sure
whether it is constrained by the stipulation with respect to the appeals
16

ID-JFO-2020-006, -013, -023, -030, -035 thru -066
before the Hearings Division, or if it has the right to decide whether to
stipulate to a new stay in the IBLA proceedings, or oppose a stay petition.
This uncertainty is resolved by recognizing the body that has jurisdiction
over the entirety of the appeals pertaining to the JRS Properties decisions
for the Coonskin-EJD and Pigtail Butte allotments—IBLA.
JRS Motion at 3-4.
The simple answer to this argument is that the six Group 2 dockets were
consolidated with both the Group 1 appeals and the Group 2 appeals, so they remain
pending before this Tribunal as part of the Group 2 consolidated appeals and this
Tribunal has jurisdiction over them. What course of action BLM may choose before the
IBLA is not at issue in this proceeding. THEREFORE, THE JRS MOTION IS DENIED.
Acting First Judge Supervisory
See page 18 for distribution.

WWP Summary Decision
BACKGROUND
The Devil Creek Group I Final Decisions on appeal herein were preceded
historically by lengthy litigation between Appellant, Western Watersheds Project
(“WWP”), and the Respondent, Bureau of Land Management (“BLM”). The Jarbidge
Field Office covers some 1.7 million acres of public and private lands in south/central
Idaho. Prior to 2015, the 1987 Jarbidge Resource Management Plan covered the
10

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
allotments that are the subject of the instant Group 1 consolidated appeals, referenced
by docket numbers above. Beginning in 2004, BLM began issuing a number of
temporary non-renewable (“TNR”) grazing permits which did not include
environmental analyses, nor public comment. BLM was administratively preparing
some five Environmental Assessments (“EA”), but the TNRs were issued without the
support of EAs.
Subsequently, WWP sued BLM in the Federal District Court for the District of
Idaho, alleging that the grazing increases included in the TNRs violated NEPA and
FLPMA. The court subsequently issued a decision in WWP’s favor determining that the
TNR permits were unlawfully issued and ultimately issued an injunction, which
terminated grazing on some 28 allotments until BLM issued a new EIS, as well as, new
grazing decisions., WWP v. Bennett, Case No. 1:04-cv-00181-BLW, ECF No. 67 (D. Idaho
Aug. 25, 2004), pp. 24-27. Subsequently, WWP, BLM, Simplot Livestock Company and
Brackett Ranches, Inc. executed a Stipulated Settlement Agreement on September 30,
2005, which was approved by the court. Thereunder, BLM was to prepare a full EIS
covering the entire Jarbidge Resource Area, which was to be the basis for revising and
updating the Jarbidge RMP and for the ultimate issuance of new grazing decisions.
BLM invited scoping comments with respect to amendments of the RMP and conducted
range studies in 2006. In March 2007, BLM issued its “Analysis of the Management
Situation for the Jarbidge Resource Management Plan” (“Jarbidge AMS”). BER 014638-
015018.
Then, in 2007 the Murphy Complex Fire burned some 426,000 acres within the
area of the Jarbidge Field Office, 64 % of which were in the Devil Creek Subregion.
Revised EA, p. 132; BER 042616. The fire had major impacts upon vegetation and
wildlife, including sage-grouse nesting habitats and sage-grouse leks. That fire was
followed by the Long Butte Fire and the 2012 Kinyon Road Fire, and largely, as a result
of those interruptions, BLM did not issue its Record of Decision for the revised Jarbidge
RMP until September 2015, which was then followed by the multi-state Approved
Resource Management Plan Amendments for Sage-Grouse (“2015 ARMPA”).
In the updated Jarbidge RMP, BLM increased the number of AUMs from 189,000
in the 1987 RMP to some 326,000 AUMs in the 2015 RMP. This was done based on data
reflecting large quantities of available forage for livestock under the vegetation
allocations, but with low levels of utilization. 2015 Jarbidge RMP, pp. 18-19; BER
018847-48. BLM and the U.S. Forest Service developed the 2015 ARMPA in response to
the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service determination in 2010 under the Endangered Species
Act that listing Greater Sage-grouse was warranted but precluded for listing because of
higher government priorities. 75 Fed. Reg. 13910, March 23, 2010. The Idaho ARMPA
11

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
established a three-tier management system for sage-grouse habitat based upon relative
habitat importance, as follows: (1) priority habitat management areas (“PHMA”),
which have the highest habitat value for maintaining sustainable sage-grouse
populations; (2) important habitat management areas (“IHMA”), which provide a
buffer for and which connect PHNA’s; and, (3) general habitat management areas
(“GHMA”), which are occupied seasonally or year-round outside of PHMAs. 2015
Record of Decision, pp. 2-8; BER 017009. The management areas are based on the State
of Idaho’s key habitat maps, which identify areas necessary for sage-grouse
conservation. BER 010710-711. Most of the Devil Creek Subregion is mapped as IHMA.
Revised EA, pp. 151-152; BER 042635-36. Because the relevant triggers in the 2015
ARMPA have been exceeded, the IHMA areas are actually managed by BLM as if they
were PHMA areas. Ibid.
In order to process new grazing permits, in 2016 the Jarbidge Field Office
divided its 1.7 million-acre territory into subregions, based upon similar topography
and related management issues. The Devil Creek Subregion was the first to be analyzed
by BLM under the auspices of the Devil Creek Subregion Livestock Grazing Permit
Renewal EA, which covers 29 separate allotments including some 357,806 acres of land.
Revised EA, p. 122; BER 042606. In preparing its EA, BLM analyzed rangeland health
data gathered between 2012 and 2016, which was incorporated into rangeland health
assessments in 2017, which, in turn, became the bases for the alternatives that were
analyzed in the Revised EA. Revised EA, pp. 2-4, BER 042485-042487. BLM analyzed
six alternatives in detail, and an additional three in lesser detail, in order to assess the
impacts of fires and livestock grazing over a period of time. The six main alternatives
analyzed were the following: (1) a no action alternative which implicated a
continuation of the previously existing management scheme; (2) the permittee
proposed management schemes; (3) management based on vegetation production; (4)
management based on vegetation production modified to include resource limitations;
(5) a reduction in grazing levels; and, (6) a no grazing option. Revised EA, pp. 12-15;
BER 041812-15. The alternatives considered, but not analyzed in detail were the
following: (1) infrastructure projects, such as, wells, water pipelines, and fences; (2)
deferment of grazing schedules; and, (3) changes in seasons of use. Revised EA. Pp.
114-116; BER 041914-16.
On August 21, 2019, BLM published the Proposed EA along with the Proposed
Decisions for all of the subject subregion allotments. Generally speaking, the field
manager determined that wildfire-related conditions could be improved over the
course of the ten-year permits by increasing livestock grazing levels in areas where non-
native grass species crowded out native vegetation, thereby allowing sagebrush
communities to re-expand. BLM received 12 protests of the Proposed Decisions from
12

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
grazing permittees, two protests from WWP and Wildlands Defense, and one protest
from the Idaho Cattle Association. In response, BLM amended the Proposed EA,
resulting in the Revised EA issued on February 28, 2020, with its accompanying FONSI.
Revised EA, pp. 2-3; BER 042485-042486. The Final Decisions for seventeen of the
subject allotments were issued on February 28, 2020. The Final Decisions for the
remaining eleven allotments in Group 2 were issued on June 15, 2020.
STANDARD OF SUMMARY JUDGMENT REVIEW
To obtain Summary Judgment there must be no substantive, material issue of
fact in dispute, and the issues for adjudication must be legal in content. Larson v. BLM,
129 IBLA 250, 252 (1994). Generally speaking, the Departmental Cases Hearings
Division, as well as, the Interior Board of Land Appeals, follow the rules of summary
judgment set out under Rule 56 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, under which all
factual inferences must be drawn in the light most favorable to the non-moving party,
drawing all reasonable inferences in its favor. Dannelle and Chad Hensley, et al., 195
IBLA 345, 354 (2020). Summary judgment is authorized where the evidence establishes
that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and where the moving party is
entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Anderson v.Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242,
247 (1986).
Once the moving party has met its burden, the burden then shifts to the non-
moving party to set forth by affidavit, or other means, specific facts showing that there
is a genuine issue of material fact or that, legally, the moving party is not entitled to
judgment. T.W. Electric Service Inc. v. Pacific Electric Contractors Association, 809 F.2d
626, 630 (9th Cir. 1987). Legal memoranda are not evidence and do not create issues of
fact capable of defeating an otherwise valid motion for summary judgment. British
Airways Board v. Boeing Company, 585 F.2d 946, 952 (9th Cir. 1987).
CONTENTIONS OF WWP
With respect to the relationship between grazing, invasive species and wildfires,
WWP states the following, “Grazing has many impacts on sage-steppe ecology and
wildlife, both widespread and localized. However, the most significant long-term
impacts result from the interaction between grazing, invasive annual grasses, and
wildfire. Livestock grazing makes sage-steppe communities more susceptible to
wildfire and annual grass invasion by suppressing native bunchgrasses, and by
damaging biological soil crusts.” WWP’s Opening Summary Judgment Brief (“WWP
SJM”), p. 18; citing the Declaration of J. Boone Kauffman, Para. 10. Generally speaking,
WWP disagrees with BLM’s determination that sage-steppe ecosystems within the
13

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
Devil Creek Subregion are grazing adapted and that the grazing increases approved in
the subject Final Decisions will help to restore native vegetation. WWP argues to the
contrary that livestock grazing causes cheatgrass dominance of sage-steppe ecosystems,
and, relatedly, WWP contends that wildfires convert native sage-steppe and native
grasslands into invasive annual grasslands. WWP SJM, p. 20; Kauffman Declaration,
Para. 16. It is further argued that conversion of native vegetation to cheatgrass caused
by heavy livestock grazing has catastrophic impacts upon sage-grouse. WWP SJM, p.
21; Kauffman Declaration, Para. 20.
Noting that there are some 688 miles of fences within the Devil Creek Subregion,
WWP argues that impacts from fences include loss of birds through collisions,
fragmentation of habitat, habitat degradation, spread of invasive plants, and increased
perching opportunities for ravens and other predators. WWP SJM, p. 25. With respect
to riparian habitats it is contended that excessive grazing degrades riparian habitats by
changing, reducing, or eliminating vegetation. WWP SJM, p. 27; Kauffman Declaration,
Para. 27.
WWP disagrees with BLM’s basic policy determination that increased grazing in
the subregion is an effective strategy for reducing the risk of wildfire. In particular,
WWP argues the following:
The Devil Creek Group 1 Final Decisions authorize as much as 40-60%
utilization on allotments across the subregion, which is far greater than
the 25% utilization recommended for the arid West by range science
experts, and also greater than the 25-30% recommended by sage-grouse
experts. The 40-60% forage utilization authorized by BLM in the Devil
Creek Final Decision will, over the 10-year term of the grazing permits
constitute chronic overgrazing that will promote the expansion of
cheatgrass and exacerbate the livestock-cheatgrass-fire cycle … . Because
of the high utilization rates required to influence wildlife behavior,
intensive grazing for wildfire control and prevention is especially harmful
if used within intact sage-steppe habitat. At the same time, permitted
grazing with a 40-60% utilization ceiling will not significantly alter fire
behavior in the hot, dry conditions typical of fire seasons in the
intermountain West.
BLM asserts that by reducing ‘fuels’ through grazing, it is possible to
prevent or control large wildfires. However, fuels are only one of three
factors influencing fire behavior. The other two factors—weather and
topography—contribute significantly to wildfire intensity and rate of
14

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
spread. During the hot dry fire seasons characteristic of the intermountain
West, the combination of high winds, high temperatures, and low relative
humidity often lead to ‘extreme’ conditions under which fuels reductions
are not effective. Thus, grazing to reduce fuel loads will not effectively
control large wildfires.
WWP SJM, pp. 30-31; citing to Kauffman Declaration, Paras. 33, 35.
WWP contends that the subject Final Decisions contain no terms, conditions or
other directives intended to protect, restore or enhance soil crusts, and the invasion of
cheatgrass is also a substantial concern. WWP SJM, p. 32. WWP further contends that
the Final Decisions contain no terms, conditions, or thresholds intended to protect
pastures still having a significant portion of sage-steppe, other than the utilization levels
specified in those decisions, which WWP contends are inadequate for that purpose.
WWP SJM, p. 33. Relatedly, WWP contends that BLM failed to include measures to
protect some 280,767 acres of big game winter range. Ibid. WWP criticizes the
authorization of “year-round” grazing on most of the subject allotments, and argues
that “… BLM has increased grazing by over 200% while loosening restrictions on
grazing permittees.” Ibid. This would allegedly result in an increase in the “… already
inflated livestock use, up to a maximum of 45,265 AUMs across 15 of the 24 Group 1
allotments.” Ibid.
WWP argues that management guidelines are provided exclusively for forage
utilization levels without including habitat-related standards, guidelines, or thresholds
as required in the 2015 ARMPA. WWP SJM, p. 34. Monitoring requirements are
contended to be inadequate, because, “At most BLM will monitor utilization and
herbaceous cover once every three years. But this frequent (relatively speaking)
monitoring is provided for on only nine allotments. On the others, monitoring will
occur on a five-year interval, or longer. In many cases, BLM is required to monitor only
utilization and herbaceous cover. More in-depth monitoring methods and assessments
of the functioning condition of riparian areas are called for only once every ten years.”
Ibid. WWP points out that none of the allotments in Group 1 are meeting all applicable
standards for rangeland health, contending that in many cases grazing is the primary
cause. WWP SJM, p. 35.
Based upon the above-referenced considerations, WWP argues that the Group 1
decisions required the preparation of a full-EIS, not just an EA. Contending that the
decisions implicate significant environmental impacts, WWP argues that the EA and
Decisions/FONSIs here violate NEPA, 42 U.S.C. 4321-4370h (2016), in several respects.
First, in light of the enormous area covered, resource values at stake, and uncertainty
15

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
about the effects of the new grazing regime, WWP argues that it was arbitrary and
capricious for BLM to conclude that the decisions would have “no significant impact;”
instead, a full EIS was required. Second, WWP argues that the EA failed to take a” hard
look” at the environmental impacts of the grazing and range improvements authorized.
Third, it is alleged that the final Revised EA does not present its analyses or conclusions
in a clear or understandable manner, and it is, therefore, allegedly difficult to tell which
actions are being considered as part of any alternative. Fourth, it is alleged that BLM
failed to consider the full effects of the alternative it actually adopted because its
various decisions selected elements of numerous different alternatives, the combined
effects of which BLM allegedly never analyzed. And, finally, WWP contends that BLM
failed to consider the cumulative impacts of the 200% grazing increases authorized
across the Jarbidge Field Office. WWP SJM, pp. 37-38. These contentions led WWP to
recommend the preparation of a full EIS.
With respect to the Revised EA itself, WWP contends that, “The Revised final EA
flunks the hard look test because it does not actually analyze the effects of the various
combinations of alternatives adopted in the Decisions; does not present its analysis in a

significant environmental effects associated with the 200 percent grazing increases by
relying on faulty assumptions and a flawed approach.” WWP SJM, p. 42. WWP argues
that BLM failed to adequately consider the impacts of the alternatives that were
adopted, citing: 40 C.F.R. 1502.14, 1502.16(d). WWP argues that the effects analyses
and the alternatives analyses under NEPA are linked and that BLM did not take the
required “hard look” because it allegedly did not conduct analyses which allowed the
public and the agency to understand the effects of the alternatives it did adopt in

DISCUSSION
With respect to NEPA compliance, Section 102(2)(C) requires consideration of the
potential impacts of a federal agency’s proposed action in a full EIS if that action is
“major” and “significantly” affects the quality of the environment. 42 U.S.C. 4332(2)(C).
A BLM decision approving an action based on an EA and FONSI will be approved if
BLM has taken the requisite “hard look” at the proposed action and identified relevant
areas of environmental concern such that it can make an informed determination that
the proposal’s impacts are insignificant or will be reduced to insignificance by the
adoption of appropriate mitigation measures. Oregon Chapter of the Sierra Club, 172
IBLA 27, 46-47 (2007); Biodiversity Conservation Alliance, 169 IBLA 321, 331 (2006). To
prevail in challenging BLM’s Final Decisions on NEPA grounds, WWP must prove by a
preponderance of the evidence that the Revised EA does not support the accompanying
FONSI because the EA contains an error of law, a demonstratable error of fact, or fails
to consider a substantial environmental question of material significance. Escalante
Wilderness Project v. BLM, 176 IBLA 300, 303 (2009); Wilderness Watch, 176 IBLA 75, 87
(2008). However, “Mere differences of opinion provide no basis for reversal of BLM’s
action if it is reasonable and supported by the record on appeal.” Smigel v. BLM, 155
IBLA 158, 166 (2001). BLM is required by Section 102(2)(E) of NEPA to consider
appropriate alternatives to its proposed action, as well as their environmental
consequences. Appropriate alternatives are defined by IBLA, as follows, “Appropriate
alternatives are those that are reasonable alternatives to the proposed action, will
accomplish its intended purpose, are technically and economically feasible, and yet
have a lesser or no impact.” The Wilderness Workshop, 175 IBLA 124, 135 (2008).
Similarly, IBLA has stated that, “A ‘rule of reason’ applies to both the range of
alternatives that must be considered and the extent to which each alternative must be
20

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
addressed.” Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 182 IBLA 377, 390-91 (2012); 40 C.F.R.
1500.2(e), 1508.9(b).
BLM enjoys broad discretion with respect to its management of public range
lands. This authority has been elucidated in numerous precedential decisions issued by
IBLA. Among those is the now-familiar test that a BLM grazing decision may be
reversed if and only if it is not supportable on any rational basis. Smigel, 155 IBLA at
164. Throughout their entire case-in-chief, WWP persists in the apparent presumption
that the “rational basis” test is a legal balancing test. It affirmatively is not a balancing
test, under which the presiding ALJ at the Hearings Division level (i.e. the trial level)
would enjoy the authority to weigh the views of conflicting experts and conflicting
documentary evidence and to conclude that the party with the higher percentage of
such evidence would win. The controlling IBLA precedent does not authorize the
undersigned to apply such a balancing test. To the contrary, if BLM proves “any
rational basis” for its grazing decision, then, under the Smigel precedent, the
undersigned is mandated to affirm BLM’s decision. And, upon close review, WWP’s
arguments constitute mere differences of opinion and differences of policy with respect
to the Final Decisions on appeal herein. WWP has presented insufficient evidence to
meet its burden of proof in a Taylor Grazing Act appeal, namely that it must prove its
case by a preponderance of the evidence. Kelly v. BLM, 131 IBLA 146 (1994); Eason v.
BLM, 127 IBLA 259, 262-63 (1993). As such, an Appellant must show not just that the
results of BLM’s analyses and ensuing conclusions could be in error, but that they are,
in fact, erroneous. BLM v. Western Watersheds Project, 191 IBLA 144, 180-181 (2017).
WWP has not met this test. And, under the Smigel “rational basis” test, I do not enjoy
the discretionary legal authority to reverse BLM’s Final Decisions on appeal herein,
because BLM proved a clear, rational basis for each of those decisions, namely, that the
increased grazing levels authorized in the Final Decisions would, in fact, reduce fine
fuels leading to a reduction in wildfires with resulting long-term improvement in range
conditions. Consequently, for these and related reasons discussed below, WWP’s
Motion For Summary Judgment must be denied.
Basically WWP’s appeal comes down to its underlying contention that only
substantial reductions in livestock grazing on the subject allotments will reduce the
continued expansion of cheatgrass and other noxious and invasive plants, thereby
allegedly fostering ecological conditions to generally improve with a related, ensuing
long, term reduction in wildfires. BLM, to the contrary, contends that its authorization
of grazing increases will serve to reduce so-called fine fuels, which will be grazed
down, thereby reducing the risk of wildfires that have historically plagued the Group 1
allotments. Burk Flat Allotment Final Decision (which is utilized as an exemplary model
decision re this and other issues on appeal herein) , pp. 43-71, BER 042813-042841.

CONCLUSION
The Jarbidge Field Manager relied upon the input and advice of the multi-person
interdisciplinary team that evaluated resources on the subject allotments and also
assisted in the drafting of the EA and FONSI. As IBLA has stated, “A party challenging
BLM’s reliance on the professional opinion of its experts must show their opinion to be
arbitrary and capricious or, by a preponderance of the evidence, that it was based on a
material error in methodology, data, analysis or conclusion. … Conclusory allegations
of error or a mere difference of professional opinion will not suffice to show BLM erred
in relying on the professional opinion of its experts.” BLM v. Western Watersheds
Project, 191 IBLA 144, 180-181 (2017).
Consequently, for the above-stated factual and legal reasons, WWP’s Motion For
Summary Judgment is DENIED; BLM’s Motion For Summary Judgment is GRANTED;
and BLM’s Final Decisions on appeal herein are APPROVED.

BLM’s Motion for Summary Judgment Granted;
WildLands Defense’s Appeals Dismissed
I. Summary
WildLands Defense (WLD) has appealed 17 Final Decisions dated February
28, 2020, and issued by the Field Manager of the Jarbidge Field Office (JFO), Bureau
of Land Management (BLM). The Final Decisions renew, with modifications, the
grazing permits for numerous grazers holding permits for grazing allotments within
the Devil Creek subregion of the JFO’s jurisdiction.
Now pending and fully briefed are cross-motions for summary judgment
filed by WLD and BLM. Also pending are cross-motions for summary judgment
regarding appeals of the Final Decisions filed by Western Watersheds Project
(WWP) and grazers, but those motions are addressed in separate Orders.
11

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Historically, the Devil Creek subregion was vegetated with sage-
shrub/bunchgrass vegetation communities. Currently, its vegetation is primarily
non-native grasslands, the chief causal factors being repeated wildfires and post-fire
seedings with crested wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass. In addition, non-native
annual grasses such as cheatgrass, are common, providing fine fuels that exacerbate
wildfire spread.
Drawing from the management outlined in the 2015 Jarbidge Resource
Management Plan (2015 RMP), the BLM elected to manage livestock grazing in the
subregion to reduce fine fuels and create openings for extant shrub communities to
expand. Therefore, the Final Decisions increase grazing levels, sometimes
substantially, to in turn increase utilization levels and expand livestock distribution
to better reduce non-native plant species. This, coupled with vegetation treatments
to restore vegetative resilience, are the means BLM outlined in its 2015 RMP to
improve rangeland conditions over the life of the RMP.
In a single Statement of Reasons (SOR) for appeal of all the Final Decisions,
WLD asserts that BLM’s management reflected in the Final Decisions will lead to
further degradation of an already degraded landscape. It argues the only avenue to
improve conditions is to significantly reduce grazing levels; remove infrastructure
such as fences, pipelines and troughs; and re-introduce native plant species. WLD
also alleges that BLM failed to comply with the National Environmental Policy Act
(NEPA), Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), and grazing
regulations.
However, WLD—which has the burden of demonstrating that BLM’s Final
Decisions lack a rational basis or that BLM has not substantially complied with the
law—has failed to adduce specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue of
material fact or that legally, BLM is not entitled to judgment. Therefore, BLM’s
motion for summary judgment must be granted, WLD’s motion for summary
judgment is denied, and WLD’s appeals are dismissed.
II. General Background
Within the area under the jurisdiction of the JFO (JFO Area) are 1.7 million
acres of public and private lands in southcentral Idaho, including 93 grazing
allotments. The area includes 911,000 acres of habitat for sage-grouse, a BLM special
status species, 600,000 acres of which has been burned by wildfire in recent years.
12

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
With respect to the 357,816-acre Devil Creek subregion, wildfire is the
primary factor influencing vegetation composition and wildlife habitats in the
subregion. Between 1993 and 2013, approximately 284,160 acres (80 percent) of
BLM-managed lands in the subregion burned at least once. Of the total burned area,
approximately half (141,390 acres) burned more than once. Wildfire activity was
particularly large in scope during the period of 2007 through 2012, when the
Murphy Complex Fire and other large fires burned over 800,000 acres within the
JFO Area, including 403,560 acres within the Devil Creek subregion (some areas
burned more than once).
Much of the subregion was historically populated with sagebrush steppe
plant communities. The subregion is currently dominated by herbaceous vegetation
largely as the result of past fire, due to either post-fire grass and forb seeding or
natural recovery of native or seeded species.
Grazing management in the JFO Area is the product of over 15 years of
litigation between WWP, grazing permittees, and the BLM. In a 2005 settlement
addressing that litigation, the BLM agreed to (1) undertake a revision of the 1987
Jarbidge Rangeland Management Plan (RMP); (2) fully process new permits for all
allotments in the JFO Area with new environmental analyses to address the impact
of grazing and associated infrastructure; and (3) implement grazing management as
described in the settlement agreement in the interim between the approval of the
settlement agreement and the issuance of final grazing decisions. See Final Decision1
at 2 (e.g., BER 042772) (summarizing the litigation).
In September 2015, BLM issued its record of decision for the Jarbidge RMP,
which was amended a week later by the multi-state Approved Resource
Management Plan Amendments for Sage-grouse (2015 ARMPA). Vegetation is the
driving focus of the 2015 RMP. Management under the plan is directed at shifting
vegetative communities from native and non-native perennial (such as crested
wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass) grasslands and annual grasses (such as
cheatgrass) towards shrublands with perennial grass understories. One way to do
so is for BLM to take interim steps to reduce fine fuels and open spaces in dense
grassland communities to allow sagebrush to spread.
1 The Final Decisions share common content and most citations to “Final Decision”
herein are to that shared common content. Therefore, one decision was selected for
citations purposes, the Buck Flat Final Decision, and citations herein to “Final
Decision” are to that final decision, unless otherwise noted.
13

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Thus, in the 2015 RMP, BLM increased its livestock allocation from

IV. Discussion
A. Standards for Summary Judgment and Burden of Proof
Although the regulations do not specifically authorize motions for summary
judgment, the Interior Board of Land Appeals (IBLA) has long recognized the
20

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
procedure as an appropriate means for resolving issues without a hearing. Larson v.
BLM, 129 IBLA 250, 252 (1994); Stamatakis v. BLM, 115 IBLA 69, 74 (1990). Federal
courts provide that a party is entitled to summary judgment if there are no genuine
issues of material fact and, as a matter of law, summary judgment is appropriate.
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322-23 (1986) (construing Rule 56 of the Federal
Rules of Civil Procedure).
In considering this question, this Tribunal must view the record evidence in
the light most favorable to the non-moving party, drawing all reasonable inferences
in its favor. Dannelle and Chad Hensley, et al., 195 IBLA 345, 354 (2020). Because WLD
has the ultimate substantive burden of proof in a challenge to BLM grazing
decisions, id. at 346, BLM, as the moving party on its summary judgment motion,
need only point out that there is an absence of evidence to support the case of WLD,
the nonmoving party. Celotex Corp., 477 U.S. at 323.
Once the moving party has met its burden, the burden then shifts to the non-
moving party to set forth by affidavit, or other means, specific facts showing that
there is a genuine issue of material fact or that legally, the moving party is not
entitled to judgment. T. W. Elec. Serv. Inc. v. Pac. Elec. Contractors Ass’n, 809 F.2d 626,
630 (9th Cir. 1987). Legal memoranda are not evidence and do not create issues of
fact capable of defeating an otherwise valid motion for summary judgment. British
Airways Bd. V. Boeing Co., 585 F2d 946, 952 (9th Cir. 1978).
Although Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56, the Federal
summary judgment rule, does not apply to the Board or the
Departmental Cases Hearings Division, statements of the burden of
proof by Federal courts applying that rule serve as useful guidance to
the Board and ALJs. For example, the Supreme Court has explained
that appellants attempting to satisfy their burden to identify genuine
issues of material fact must set forth specific facts showing the
existence of such an issue and may not simply rest on mere allegations
or denials “without ‘any significant probative evidence tending to
support’” their claims. Evidence that is “merely colorable” or “not
significantly probative” is insufficient to defeat summary judgment.
. . . A “material” fact is one which “might affect the outcome of the suit
under the governing law.” This in turn “necessarily implicates the
substantive evidentiary standard of proof” and requires the ALJ (and
21

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
this Board) to “view the evidence presented through the prism of the
substantive evidentiary burden.” . . .
To determine whether an alleged fact might affect the outcome
and thus be material, it must be examined in view of the highly
deferential standard of review applicable to BLM grazing decisions. It
is well-established that BLM “enjoys broad discretion in determining
how to manage and adjudicate grazing preferences” on BLM managed
lands, “to do any and all things necessary to . . . provide for the orderly
use, improvement, and development of the [Federal] range,” and “to
preserve the land and its resources from destruction or unnecessary
injury.” This, in turn, results in a highly deferential standard of review
for BLM decisions adjudicating grazing privileges. By regulation,
“[n]o adjudication of grazing preference will be set aside on appeal, if
it appears that it is reasonable and that it represents a substantial
compliance with the provisions of part 4100 of” Title 43 of the Code of
Federal Regulations. The appellant bears the burden of establishing,
by a preponderance of the evidence, that the challenged BLM decision
fails to substantially comply with the statute and its implementing
regulations, or that the decision is unreasonable and lacks a rational
basis. The Department has thus “considerably narrowed the scope of
review of BLM grazing decisions by an [ALJ] and by this Board” to
whether the appellant has established that the challenged decision “is
not supportable on any rational basis.”
The Board also follows the “longstanding principle that an
appellant’s burden to demonstrate error in a BLM grazing decision,
founded on the professional opinion of BLM’s experts, will ‘not [be]
carried by mere expressions of disagreement with BLM’s analysis and
conclusions.’” Likewise, “[i]t is well settled that BLM is entitled to rely
on the professional opinion of its experts concerning matters within
the realm of their expertise, where it is reasonable and supported by
record evidence,” and “‘[w]hen specialists express conflicting views,
an agency must have discretion to rely on the reasonable opinions of
its own qualified experts.’” Therefore, “[a] party challenging BLM’s
evaluation must do more than offer a contrary opinion” or show “that
a different course of action or interpretation is available and supported
by the evidence.” Rather, in challenging

[an appellant] must show their opinion to be arbitrary
and capricious or, by a preponderance of the evidence,
that it was based on a material error in methodology,
data, analysis or conclusion. It must show, with objective
evidence, either “BLM erred when collecting the
underlying data, when interpreting that data, or when

Under this formulation,
the challenging party “must show not just that the results

BLM may prepare an EA to assist its determination of whether
an EIS is required, or to aid the agency’s decision-making when an EIS
is not necessary. BLM issues a FONSI when it determines that an EIS
is not necessary. An EA is “a concise public document” that includes
“brief discussions” of essential elements of the impacts analysis at a
level of depth and detail normally “limited to the minimum needed to
determine whether there would be significant environmental effects”
from the proposed action. We have consistently held that “[a]n EA
need not discuss the merits and drawbacks of the proposal in
exhaustive detail” as “[b]y its nature, it is intended to be an overview
of environmental concerns, not an exhaustive study of all
environmental issues”; accordingly, “[s]o long as an EA contains a
‘reasonably thorough discussion of . . . significant aspects of the
probable environmental consequences,’ NEPA requirements have
been satisfied.”
In evaluating the adequacy of an EA, the Board is guided by a
“rule of reason” and will generally find that BLM has taken the
requisite “hard look” when its conclusion that no significant
environmental impact exists is founded on a reasoned evaluation of
relevant factors that is documented in the record. “An appellant
challenging the adequacy of an EA has the burden of demonstrating
with objective evidence that the assessment is premised on a clear
error of law or demonstrable error of fact, or that the analysis failed to
consider a substantial environmental question of material significance
to the proposed action.” This burden is not satisfied by speculation,
conclusory allegations unsupported by evidence, or mere differences
of opinion regarding the likelihood or significance of environmental
impacts. Nor are disagreements or presentations of different points of
view over the preferable course of action sufficient absent connection
to an affirmative showing that BLM failed to consider a substantial
environmental question of material significance. The fact “[t]hat an
appellant has a different opinion about the likelihood or significance
of environmental impacts or prefers that BLM take another course of
action does not establish that BLM violated the procedural
requirements of NEPA.”

BLM is entitled to rely on the professional opinions of its

analysis, or conclusion of the expert. Such opinions are entitled to
considerable deference, and “[a] mere difference of opinion, even of
expert opinion, will not suffice to show that BLM failed to fully
comprehend the true nature, magnitude, or scope of the likely

Regulations implementing NEPA require that a Federal agency
consider the potential cumulative impacts of a planned action together
with other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions.

incremental impact of the action when added to other
past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions
regardless of what agency (Federal or non-Federal) or
person undertakes such other actions. Cumulative
impacts can result from individually minor but
collectively significant actions taking place over a period
of time.

70 (1992). In arguing that cumulative impacts were overlooked,

17 of the Devil Creek Subregion grazing decisions in early 2020 and the remaining

impact of the alternatives on resources located on the various allotments and
considered cumulative effects in a manner that fully disclosed the effects of grazing
in conjunction with past, present and reasonably foreseeable future actions. BLM

including avoiding key locations and periods, such as sage-grouse leks, lekking
season, and nesting habitat. Revised EA 2.4 at 18 (BER 042502). In response to a
WWP protest about range infrastructure, BLM noted that “[n]ew range
infrastructure will be placed in previously disturbed areas where practical and
infrastructure that currently conflicts with sage-grouse habitat priorities will be
moved or modified, consistent with direction in the 2015 RMP, as amended by the
ARMPA.” Final Decision, Response to Protest Point 13/2c, at 51-52 (BER 042821-
042822). Overall, fencing decreases under the Final Decisions for the subregion, as
some fencing will be removed. Final Decision, Response to Protest Point 13/4a, at 65
(BER 042835). In sum, BLM took a “hard look” at the impacts of range
infrastructure.
F. WLD’s FLPMA Claims
WLD contends that BLM violated FLPMA in several ways. First, BLM
allegedly failed to comply with the applicable land use plan: the 2015 RMP, as
modified by the ARMPA. FLPMA mandates that BLM “shall manage the public
lands . . . in accordance with the land use plans, 43 U.S.C. § 1732(a) (2012), and the
implementing regulations require “conformance” to the land use plans, 43 C.F.R. §
4100.0-8. Conformance “means that a resource management action . . . shall be
clearly consistent with” the land use plans. 43 C.F.R. § 1601.0-5(b).
55

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Second, WLD argues that BLM violated FLPMA’s mandate to “take any
action necessary to prevent unnecessary or undue degradation of the lands.” 43
U.S.C. § 1732(b).
Federal courts have opined that the broad language in FLPMA
directing BLM to prevent unnecessary or undue degradation "'leaves
[the] BLM a great deal of discretion in deciding how to achieve" this
objective. And [the] Board has interpreted "unnecessary or undue
degradation" to generally mean the occurrence of "something more
than the usual effects anticipated" from appropriately mitigated
development.
WildLands Defense, 192 IBLA at 405.
Third, WLD maintains that BLM did not comply with FLPMA’s mandate to
manage lands under the principle of multiple use, 43 U.S.C. § 1732(a), which
requires that BLM informedly and rationally balance competing resource values to
ensure that public lands are managed in the manner “that will best meet the present
and future needs of the American people.” National Wildlife Federation v. BLM, 140
IBLA 85, 101 (1997) (quoting 43 U.S.C. § 1702(c)). To show error in a BLM multiple-
use determination, an appellant must demonstrate that BLM’s weighing of the
resource values was unreasonable, Bristlecone Alliance et al., 179 IBLA 51, 58 (2010),
i.e., that BLM did not engage in a reasoned and informed decision-making process.
WildLands Defense, 192 IBLA at 404.
BLM complied with FLPMA because the Final Decisions are consistent with
the 2015 RMP, as amended, and comply with FLPMA's directives to manage public
lands under the principle of multiple use and to prevent unnecessary or undue
degradation. WLD has not met its burden to show that BLM erred.
WLD asserts that BLM violated a litany of provisions in the 2015 RMP, as
amended. WLD MSJ at 43-45. WLD once again asserts, among other things, that
BLM lacked adequate baseline data so that BLM cannot ensure compliance with the
RMP. Id. at 12. BLM concluded that the Final Decisions comply with the 2015 RMP,
as amended, and, as previously noted, WLD has provided no evidence showing that
BLM's experts failed to adequately assess the likely impacts of the Final Decisions,
given baseline conditions, or that additional information on baseline conditions
would have demonstrably altered BLM's analysis of likely impacts.
56

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
WLD particularly focuses on the assertion that the Final Decisions do not
conform to provisions in the 2015 RMP, as amended, requiring BLM to conserve,
maintain and restore sage-grouse. However, WLD barely addresses the Revised
EA's extensive discussions of the potential impacts on sage-grouse, except with
general references to scientific studies viewed as favorable to its positions but
unmoored to any analysis of their application to the specific allotment conditions
and grazing management. Nor does it give consideration to the best management
practices and other measures required by the Final Decisions to protect sage-grouse
and its habitat.
BLM is not required by the 2015 RMP, as amended, to avoid every adverse
effect on sage grouse or its habitat; the fact that some of the measures to be
implemented may adversely affect sage grouse or specific areas of its habitat - as
BLM disclosed in the Revised EA - does not show that the Final Decisions fail to
conform to the 2015 RMP, as amended. See WildLands Defense, 192 IBLA at 404.
BLM convincingly responded to several protest points alleging that it did not
comply with the 2015 RMP, as amended, see, e.g., Final Decision, Responses to
Protest Points 13/1c, 13/4, 13/4b, and 14/1, at 47, 55-56, 68-69, 71-72 (BER 042817,
042825-26, 042838-39, 042841-42), and WLD has not offered argument or proof
contradicting those responses.
The ID Team recommended grazing management in the Final Decisions that
would provide for the habitat needs of sage-grouse. Final Decision, Response to
Protest Point 13/2c, at 51 (BER 042821). The Final Decisions provide for increases in
grazing to reduce the threat of wildfire and competition from non-native grasses
damaging to the sagebrush communities on which sage-grouse and other species
depend. Furthermore, the increases top out at moderate grazing levels, with other
measures to minimize adverse impacts and improve range conditions. BLM’s
approach is consistent with the 2015 RMP, which contemplates increases in grazing
from the previous RMP allocations and contains the livestock grazing goal (LG-G-2)
to use livestock grazing “to support maintenance and restoration of resilient
ecosystem structure and function[.]”
In sum, WLD assertions that the Final Decisions do not comply with the 2015
RMP, as amended, are conclusory and unsupported. They merit no further
discussion.
WLD, in asserting that the Final Decisions will cause undue degradation in
violation of FLPMA, raises the same conclusory and unsupported arguments as to
57

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
why the Final Decisions allegedly are not rational. WLD relies again on its claim
that the baseline data is deficient to argue that this deficiency prevents a clear-
reasoned, science-based analysis of the undue degradation the Final Decisions will
cause, increasing the likelihood of undue degradation. Id. at 13, 15. BLM concluded
that no undue degradation would occur and, as previously noted, WildLands
Defense has provided no evidence showing that BLM's experts failed to adequately
assess the likely impacts of the Final Decisions, given baseline conditions, or that
additional information on baseline conditions would have demonstrably altered
BLM's analysis of likely impacts.
WLD asserts that undue degradation will not be prevented because the
thresholds and responses are optional, id. at 15, but, in fact, BLM is mandated to take
responsive action when a threshold is exceeded. WLD references the lack of a
carrying capacity determination as significant, id. at 37, but, as previously discussed,
a quantitative calculation of carrying capacity determination is not required before
issuing or renewing a grazing permit and WLD doesn’t demonstrate why it’s
required to comply with the 2015 RMP. WLD asserts that grazing management in
the Final Decisions amounts to “outcome-based” grazing which violates the grazing
regulations and FLPMA, id. at 21, but WLD has made no such showing that the
adaptive management constitutes such a violation.
Finally, WLD contends that undue degradation will result from drastically
increasing stocking, and permanent facilities “and other harmful actions.” WLD
MSJ at 6. WLD elaborates that
[n]ew and expanded livestock damage and injury to weed-vulnerable
uplands and riparian areas will be expanded under the extreme
stocking and chaotic management of the [Final Decisions], and the
EA’s climate change stress and species imperilment denialism ---
facility proliferation, extreme stocking rates, chaotic uncertain grazing
schemes, increased spring use in crucial habitats, targeted grazing,
unlimited amounts of supplement feeding to facilitate forage mining,
water hauling and even more inflated numbers of livestock under
potential TNR.3
3 The reference to potential TNR (temporary non-renewable grazing use) is
perplexing because the Final Decisions do not authorize TNR.
58

ID-JFO-2020-001 through -034
Id. at 9. According to WLD, “BLM blindly ignored nearly all the voluminous
information in the 2007 AMS concerning the harms to wildlife and other public
lands values that will be caused by the permittee-desired actions embraced by the
[Final Decisions]. Id. at 10; see also id. at 23.
These or nearly identical unsubstantiated conclusory arguments failed to
establish that the Final Decisions lacked a rational basis. A BLM decision will not be
found to constitute unnecessary or undue degradation so long as its conclusions
have a rational basis in the record, as they do in this case. WildLands Defense, 192
IBLA at 405; Western Watersheds Project, 188 IBLA 234, 247 (2016).
V. Conclusion
Based upon the foregoing, BLM’s motion for summary judgment regarding
WLD’s appeals of the Group 1 Final Decisions is granted; WLD’s motion for
summary judgment is denied; and the Group 1 Final Decisions on appeal herein
are affirmed. Consequently, WLD’s appeals are dismissed.
Acting First Judge Supervisory
Appeal Information
Any person who has a right to appeal under 43 C.F.R. § 4.410 or other
applicable regulation may appeal this order to the Interior Board of Land Appeals.
The notice of appeal must be filed with the office of the Administrative Law Judge
who issued the order within 30 days of receiving the order, and a copy of the notice
must be served on every other party. In accordance with 43 C.F.R. § 4.478(c), the
Board will issue an expedited briefing schedule and decide the appeal promptly.
See page 60 for distribution.

BACKGROUND
The Pigtail Butte Allotment is in the southeast portion of the Devil Creek
Subregion and includes 30,581 acres divided into eleven pastures. Guerry Final
Decision, p. 4, BER 043701. BLM administered public lands are 28,462 acres, Idaho state
lands are 1,280 acres, and there are 839 acres of private land. Revised EA, p. 6. Under
the expiring permits, the average yearly actual use in the Pigtail Butte Allotment was
2,580 AUMs, which included 1,344 AUMs on the part of JRS and 1,236 AUMs by
Guerry, Inc., with an average of 1,676 cattle grazed between March 1 and February 28
by JRS and Guerry. JRS Final Decision (June 15, 2020), p. 6.
The Coonskin-AMD Allotment is in the north central portion of the Devil Creek
Subregion and is composed of 42,809 acres divided into seven pastures. BLM public
lands are 41,054 acres, Idaho state lands are 1,281 acres, and there are 474 acres of

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
privately owned land. Revised EA, pp. 126-127. The East Juniper Draw Allotment
abuts the Coonskin Allotment to the east and is composed of 24,051 acres divided into
six pastures. BLM public lands are 20,705 acres, Idaho state lands are 1,280 acres, and
there are 2,065 acres of privately owned land. Ibid. Under the Guerry Final Decision on
appeal, Guerry is authorized to graze up to 3,255 AUMs, representing 7,821 sheep or
1,564 cattle, between March 1 and February 28 each year on pastures that composed the
former Coonskin Allotment. Guerry Final Decision, pp. 10-11. Relatedly, under the JRS
Final Decision on appeal, JRS is authorized to graze up to 2,182 cattle, 10,259 AUMs,
across the entire newly combined Coonskin-EJD Allotment from March 1 to February
28. JRS Final Decision, p. 7.
BLM also authorized the installation of range improvements to facilitate grazing.
Included are some 3.1 miles of new pipeline and three new trough sites in three
separate pastures. And, all fences within 1.2 miles of occupied lek sites must be marked
with collision diverter devices. Guerry Final Decision, pp. 18-19; JRS Final Decision, pp.
18-19.
By way of further background, BLM began the permit renewal process for the
subject allotments in the Devil Creek Subregion by reviewing the Pigtail Butte
Rangeland Health Assessment, pp. 59-136; BER 177386-177463. As pointed out in
BLM’s Motion , “The data showed that within the subregion, wildfire was the major
influencer on rangeland health. Wildfire led to significant reductions in shrub-
dominated vegetation communities … .” BLM Motion, p. 2. During the following two
years, BLM invited applications from the permittees on the subject allotments. BLM
prepared it’s Proposed EA, which analyzed the impacts of various management
alternatives on the subject allotments. Then, on August 21, 2019, the BLM published the
proposed EA along with the Proposed Decisions for all of the subject subregion
allotments. The field manager determined that wildfire-related conditions could be
improved over the course of the ten-year permits by increasing livestock grazing levels
in areas where non-native grasses crowded out native vegetation, thereby allowing
sagebrush communities to expand.
BLM received twelve protests of the Proposed Decisions from grazing

one protest from the Idaho Cattle Association. In response, BLM amended the initial

issued on February 28, 2020. The Final Decisions for the remaining eleven allotments in

STANDARD OF REVIEW FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT
To obtain Summary Judgment there must be no material, substantive issue of
fact in dispute between the parties. Larson v. BLM, 129 IBLA 250, 252 (1994). Generally
speaking, the Departmental Cases Hearings Division, as well as the Interior Board of
Land Appeals (“IBLA”), in practice follow the rules of summary judgment set out
under Rule 56 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, under which all factual
inferences must be drawn in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, drawing
all reasonable inferences in its favor. Dannelle and Chad Hensley, et al., 195 IBLA 345,
354 (2020). Summary Judgment is authorized where the evidence establishes that there
is no genuine issue as to any material fact and where the moving party, therefore, is
entitled to a judgment as a matter of law. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242,
247 (1986).
Once the moving party has met its burden, the burden then shifts to the non-
moving party to set forth by affidavit, or other means, specific facts showing that there
is a genuine issue of material fact or that, legally, the moving party is not entitled to
judgment. T.W. Electric Service, Inc. v. Pacific Electric Contractors Association, 809 F.2d
626, 630 (9th Cir. 1987). Legal memoranda are not evidence and do not create issues of
fact capable of defeating an otherwise valid motion for summary Judgment. British
Airways Board v. Boeing Company, 585 F.2d 946, 952 (9th Cir. 1987).

DISCUSSION
The Interior Board Of Land Appeals (“IBLA”), has determined the relevant
standard for review of an EA, as follows:
When BLM concludes in a FONSI that it is not necessary to prepare an EIS
and proceeds on the basis of an EA, its decision will be deemed to comply
with NEPA where the record demonstrates that BLM considered all
relevant matters of environmental concern, took a ‘hard look’ at potential
environmental impacts, and made a convincing case that no significant
impact will result or that any such impact will be reduced to
insignificance by the adoption of appropriate mitigation measures. …
In assessing the adequacy of an EA, we are guided by the ‘rule of reason’
and recognize that, in an EA, BLM need only briefly discuss the likely
impacts of the proposed action: ‘By nature, it is intended to be an
overview of environmental concerns, not an exhaustive study of all
environmental issues which the project raises.’ Since the purpose of an
EA is to assess whether the potential impacts of the proposed action
are likely to be significant, it may be a ‘concise public document’ that
‘briefly’ discusses ‘the environmental impacts of the proposed action and
alternatives.’ Thus, an EA will not be set aside ‘merely because the EA
17

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
could have been more thorough,’ because the burden is on the appellant
to show that any omitted analysis ‘compromised the EA so severely as to
render the FONSI arbitrary and capricious.’
Bureau of Land Management v. Western Watersheds Project & Wild Utah Project, 191
IBLA 144, 149-151 (2017).
Therefore, the fundamental issue becomes the following: Was the content of the
Revised EA issued in February 2020, within the four corners thereof, legally sufficient
on its face to justify the accompanying FONSI and to adequately analyze relevant
environmental issues covering all of the Group 1 and Group 2 subregion Final
Decisions? In my opinion, the answer to that question is yes, because if one completely
deletes or ignores BLM’s referenced responses to the various public comments, which
responses were included in the eleven June 2020 Final Decisions, the Revised EA
remains legally sufficient on its face, within the four corners of the Revised EA, to
support and justify the FONSI, as well as, each of the eleven June 2020 Final Decisions.
IBLA has addressed a similar issue, under analogous factual circumstances, as
follows:
In the present case, there is no issue regarding the public disclosure for
comment of data compiled regarding the impacts of the Lisbon Valley
Project leading up to and including the issuance of the FEIS and ROD.
Following issuance of the FEIS and ROD, Appellants filed their appeal,
and thereafter, new information was generated. It is this new information
that Appellants argue must be distributed for public comment
or NEPA requirements will be violated.
We disagree. The new information does not radically change an
assumption of the FEIS, or relate directly to an alternative action, or show
that there are significant impacts of the project that were not disclosed in
the FEIS. In fact, the new information confirmed the assumption of the
FEIS that the Navajo Aquifer was a Class III aquifer, and it also arguably
establishes that impacts to ground water quality will be minimal. In
addition, BLM sent copies of all the new information to Appellants and
the information was publicly available. The groundwater data and
analyses were also submitted to the State of Utah, which classified the
18

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
Navajo Aquifer as Class III. The fact that the information was not released
expressly for public comment is not, under the facts of this case, a
violation of NEPA.
National Wildlife Federation, ET AL., 145 IBLA 348, 365 (1998); emphasis added.
BLM’s Revised EA was intended to cover all of the subregion subject allotments
in both Group 1 and Group 2. BLM’s Final Decisions covering all of the allotments
were divided into two groups, Group 1 and Group 2, because of the large number of
public comments that were submitted with respect to the eleven decisions that
ultimately were included in the June 2020 Group 2. Had it not been for the large
number of public comments that were received by BLM covering the allotments in
Group 2, it is apparent that BLM would have issued all of the Final Decisions in
February 2020.
In plain terms, JRS contends that BLM’s Group 2 responses to the Group 2
permittees’ public comments regarding the Proposed Decisions, constituted additional
rationalizations that should have been included in the February 2020 Revised EA or
been addressed in a further revised, updated EA covering the Group 2 June 2020 Final
Decisions. This argument would be correct, if and only if, the February 2020 Revised
EA was, within its four corners, legally insufficient in content to environmentally
support the FONSI, as well as, both the Group 1 February 2020 Final Decisions and the
Group 2 June 2020 Final Decisions. However, it is my determination that the February
2020 Revised EA remains legally sufficient on its face, given its content, to adequately
support both the FONSI and all of the Group 1 and Group 2 Final Decisions, just as
would have been the case had no public comments been submitted by the permittees
and responded to by BLM. In particular, the Revised EA analyzes a legally sufficient
number of alternatives; the Revised EA takes the requisite “hard look” at relevant
environmental issues and impacts; and, the Revised EA includes legally sufficient
analyses of relevant cumulative impacts, covering all of the allotments in Group 1 and
Group 2. Given this, the fact that BLM went on to fully address the Group 2 public
comments did not serve to automatically negate the legal sufficiency of the Revised EA
to cover all of the Group 1 and Group 2 Final Decisions.
19

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
CONCLUSION
For the above-stated reasons, it is my determination that BLM’s February 2020
Revised EA was legally sufficient to support the associated FONSI, as well as all of the
Group 1 and Group 2 Final Decisions. Consequently, Appellant JRS’s Motion For
Summary Judgment is hereby DENIED; BLM’s Motion For Summary Judgment is
GRANTED.

BRANDAU, :

BLM’S REQUEST TO VACATE AND REMAND DECISION DENIED
On November 9, 2005, counsel of record for the Bureau of Land Management (BLM)
filed the Bureau Of Land Management’s Request To Vacate And Remand Decision. On
November 15, 2005, the undersigned issued an Order affording the Appellants and the
Intervenors until November 23, 2005, in which to file a response to said request. In turn, on
November 21, 2005, counsel of record for the Appellants filed Appellants’ Opposition To BLM’s
Motion To Vacate And Remand.
BLM’s request is premised, in part, upon the content of the Order issued by the
undersigned on July 5, 2005, which included a partial stay of the April 22, 2005, Final Decision
on appeal herein. My July 5th Order stayed only a portion of BLM’s Decision on appeal, namely,
that portion of the Decision, which authorized certain range improvement projects. My July 5th
Order did not stay the grazing system portion of BLM’s Final Decision.
BLM’s instant request to vacate, raises the procedurally interesting issue of whether or
not the Appellants are procedurally entitled to appeal and adjudicate that portion of BLM’s
Decision which was not stayed in my July 5th Order, or whether, in the alternative, BLM is
somehow automatically entitled to vacate the totality of the Bureau’s formally issued Decision,
under circumstances where the grazing portion of that Decision was not stayed. Stated somewhat
differently the issue is as follows: As a matter of procedural due process, does BLM enjoy a
unilateral, procedural right to vacate its Decision in toto, or, in the alternative, do the Appellants
and Intervenors enjoy the jurisdictional right to have the grazing portion of BLM’s Decision fully
adjudicated on the record.
Because my July 5th Order stayed only a portion of BLM’s Decision on appeal herein, the
Appellants and Intervenors enjoy a jurisdictional, procedural right to appeal and have fully
adjudicated, in an APA on-the-record hearing, the grazing portion of BLM’s Decision, which has
4

not been stayed. Under the provisions of 43 C.F.R. 4.472 (e), “Any final BLM grazing decision
that is not already in effect and for which a stay is not granted will become effective immediately
after the administrative law judge denies a petition for a stay ... .” I denied the petition for stay
with respect to the grazing portion of BLM’s Final Decision, which, therefore, became “effective
immediately.” In my Order dated October 21, 2005, which denied BLM’s earlier request for
remand in this matter, I stated the following, “Another, potential procedural avenue would be a
Motion To Vacate and Remand by BLM, which would require the concurrence of the Appellants
and Intervenors.” (Emphasis added; Order-- “BLM’s Request For Remand Denied,” October 21,
2005, p. 5). I reiterate strongly my view that for the government to vacate this docket, the
concurrence of the other parties in interest is procedurally required, because the grazing portion
of BLM’s decision is in effect under the referenced regulatory provision.
Relatedly, as a procedural matter, “Any applicant, permittee, lessee, or other person
whose interest is adversely affected by a final BLM grazing decision may appeal the decision to
an administrative law judge ... .” 43 C.F.R. 4.470. Having timely filed their original appeal, the
Appellants have a jurisdictional, procedural right to adjudicate the grazing portion of BLM’s
Decision, and BLM does not enjoy any unilateral, procedural right to subvert the appellate rights
of the Appellants through an untimely motion to vacate. Jurisdiction over BLM’s Final Decision
on appeal reposes exclusively in the Departmental Cases Hearings Division.
In this context, as Appellants correctly point out in their Opposition, BLM has known of
the scheduled hearing for months. Indeed, the hearing in this matter was the subject of a
telephone conference conducted by the undersigned on July 26, 2005, which included Kenneth
M. Sebby, Esq., on behalf of BLM; Todd C. Tucci, Esq., on behalf of the Appellants; Richard
and Connie Brandau, Intervenors; and William Watterson, Intervenor. During that conference,
the undersigned, the BLM, the Appellants, and each of the Intervenors specifically agreed to
commence the public hearing on December 12, 2005, and, if not completed, to reconvene the
hearing on January 23, 2006. The government cannot claim lack of advance notice with respect
to the scheduled hearing.
For the above-stated jurisdictional and procedural reasons, BLM’s Request To Vacate
And Remand Decision is DENIED. The public hearing in this matter will commence at 1:00
p.m. on Monday, December 12, 2005, in Caldwell, Idaho, at the place designated in the Owyhee
Field Manager’s Notice dated November 1, 2005.
James H. Heffernan
Administrative Law Judge

BRANDAU, :
